124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227:

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```
439: 
440: ---

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:

450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content

454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457:

461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.

19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.

46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).

2: title: README Template and Selection Guide
3: description: Concise guidance for project, skill, feature and component README files, with routing to the code-folder README template when developer topology is the main need.
4: trigger_phrases:

8:   - "narrative readme structure"
9: importance_tier: normal

11: version: 1.2.1.0
12: ---
13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.

14: 
15: ---
16: 
17: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
18: 
19: | Aspect | What you get |
20: |---|---|
21: | **Packet kind** | `surface`, backend `evidence-base`, read-only |
22: | **Tools** | `Read, Bash, Grep, Glob` |
23: | **Use it for** | Adding, editing or reviewing a GitHub Actions workflow, composite action or workflow script |
24: | **Invoke with** | No direct invocation. The sk-code hub bundles it beside a workflow mode when a request is about a workflow |
25: | **Advisor** | invisible (`routingClass: metadata`) |
26: | **Bundled with** | `sk-code-quality` when authoring, `sk-code-review` when reviewing |
27: | **Produces** | The rule evidence, the protected set, the exception record, the scaffold templates and a CI profile template. The packet itself edits nothing |
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. OVERVIEW
32: 
33: ### Why This Surface Exists
34: 
35: The repository's workflows follow a set of rules that live mostly in review memory. Only path parity between the two source roots is checked by a machine. SHA pinning, a README row per workflow, timeouts, least-privilege permissions, concurrency and the cached setup action are conventions that nothing enforces. Two further facts are easy to misread: a rebuild commit must not start the downstream workflows, and `.github/workflows/message-contract.yml` deliberately pushes on every branch.
36: 
37: Without one written source a reviewer cannot tell a deliberate trigger from drift, and an author starts a new workflow from a copy of the nearest one, inheriting its gaps.
38: 
39: ### What It Does
40: 
41: The packet states each rule next to the file and line that prove it and says whether anything enforces it. It lists the workflows protected by function, so a change that would weaken one asks for a second confirmation first. It records message-contract's every-branch push trigger as an intentional exception, with the reason, so a report does not flag it. It also holds a whole-workflow template and a job template that start compliant.
42: 
43: The packet never writes. The acting mode or a doctor command applies any change it recommends. `/doctor:ci report` lists every workflow with its switch state. `/doctor:ci scaffold` writes a new workflow from these templates after a yes. `/doctor:ci toggle` turns one switch variable off or back on after a yes.
44: 
45: ### The Repository Profile
46: 
47: The rules are universal, but the values they apply to are not. Branch names, switch variables, protected workflows, path twins, the workflows README and the setup action differ from one repository to the next, so the three `/doctor:ci` routes read them from a CI profile: `--profile`, then the git config value `skcode.ciProfile`, then `repository/ci.json` in this packet, then a generic default that forces none of them. This repository commits its profile, and its `SKILLED_CI*` switches, its `gate-inputs.yml` protected workflow and its `.opencode/` twin are that profile's values, not rules of the packet. A `repository` field limits the profile to the repository it names, so a copy shipped with the skills into another repository is ignored, and a file left at the former root-level `.sk-code/` path is refused rather than read, with its move named. A repository without a profile reads clean: the report requires no switch and checks no README row, the scaffold prints none of this repository's names, and the toggle accepts any variable a job compares against `off` and refuses the one behind a status check the live branch ruleset requires. `assets/ci-profile.template.json` is the starting point for a new profile.
48: 
49: ---
50: 
51: ## 3. REFERENCE MAP
52: 
53: | File | Carries |
54: |---|---|
55: | `references/ci-workflow-standards.md` | The rule index: path parity, SHA pins, README row, `set -euo pipefail`, fork and secret safety, matrix and `fail-fast` |
56: | `references/trigger-and-filter-rules.md` | The twin rule, the rebuild-commit skip rule, push-only scope and the intentional exceptions table |
57: | `references/job-shape-rules.md` | Timeouts, permissions, the concurrency template, the composite setup action and the switch `if:` shape |
58: | `references/protected-set.md` | The repository CI profile and its keys, the workflows protected by function and the rules that follow |
59: | `assets/workflow-template.yml` | Whole-workflow scaffold |
60: | `assets/job-block-template.yml` | Single-job scaffold |
61: | `assets/ci-profile.template.json` | The profile a repository fills in to give `/doctor:ci` its own conventions |
62: | `manual-testing-playbook/` | The routing scenario the hub's router-sync guard replays, and the foreign-repository scenario that runs the CI doctor against a mocked `gh` |
63: 
64: The implement, debug and verify doctrine is symlinked in from `../shared/references/`.
65: 
66: ---
67: 
68: ## 4. VERIFICATION
69: 
70: | Check | How to run it |
71: |---|---|
72: | Hub gate | `node .skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/parent-skill-check.cjs .skilled/skills/sk-code` exits 0 |
73: | Drift guards | `bash .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/scripts/run-all-drift-guards.sh` exits 0 |
74: | Compiled route | `node --test .skilled/bin/tests/compiled-route-surface-hint.test.cjs` exits 0 |

85: | [ROUTER.md](ROUTER.md) | Machine router: intent map, resource map and routing pseudocode |

31: 
32: A job with no `timeout-minutes` runs until GitHub stops it at 360 minutes, so a hang costs six hours of runner time. Size the timeout from measured runs and never guess it.
33: 
34: **Formula.** `max(<floor>, ceil(3 x job p50 minutes), ceil(2 x job p100 minutes))` with a floor of 10 minutes. Pull at least 40 recent runs of job-level timings (`gh run view --json jobs`), compute p50 and p100 per job and state the observed p100 next to the chosen value in the commit or the workflow comment. A successful job in the sample should never exceed half of its new timeout.
35:

54: ## 3. PERMISSIONS
55: 
56: Least privilege is the default. A workflow declares `permissions: contents: read` at the top, and a job widens it only for what that job needs.
57: 
58: - **Read-only workflow.** `permissions: contents: read` written as a block, as in `.github/workflows/message-contract.yml:13`.
59: - **No scope at the workflow level.** `permissions: {}` at the top and a scope on each job, as in `.github/workflows/trigger-index-rebuild.yml:12`. The rebuild job then asks for `contents: read` at `:40` and the push job asks for `actions: read` and `contents: write` at `:195-196`.

61: - **A job that holds a write scope, or pushes, checks out with `persist-credentials: false`.** The checkout then leaves no token in the git config for a later step to reuse, and the job passes its token only to the command that needs it, as in `.github/workflows/trigger-index-rebuild.yml:203`. 69: ## 4. CONCURRENCY
70: 
71: A workflow that answers to pushes and pull requests carries one group, so a newer push does not leave an older run burning minutes.
72: 
73: ```yaml
74: concurrency:
75:   group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
76:   cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
77: ```
78: 
79: The recommended default cancels a superseded run on a pull request and never cancels a run on a branch push. The alternative is `cancel-in-progress: true` on main as well, which saves more runner minutes and leaves some commits on the branch with no completed run.
80: 
81: A workflow whose runs must queue instead of cancel sets `cancel-in-progress: false` and says why. `.github/workflows/trigger-index-rebuild.yml:21-23` does, because a newer pending run replaces an older pending one and the run for the newest push is never dropped.
82: 
83: Today 32 of 32 workflows carry a `concurrency:` block. Thirty use the pull-request-only value above. Two use `false`: the rebuild workflow, and `dependabot-auto-merge.yml`, because a cancelled run could stop before it turns auto-merge on.
84: 
85: Enforcement: honour-system.
86: 
87: ---
88: 
89: ## 5. THE COMPOSITE SETUP ACTION
90: 
91: Every workflow that needs the repository's dependency trees calls one composite action instead of repeating the install and build steps. The profile's `setupAction` names it, and the job template adds the step only when the profile does. Everything below in this section is the Skilled example.
92: 
93: ```yaml
94: - name: Provision the dependency trees
95:   uses: ./.github/actions/setup
96: ```
97: 
98: The action is `.github/actions/setup/action.yml`. The rules it follows:
99: 
100: - **The key covers every lockfile plus the Node major.** The cache key is built from the runner OS, the Node major read from the runner, the bun version and a hash of every lockfile and package manifest the trees install from. A change to any of them is a different key.
101: - **No `restore-keys`.** A partial match would restore a tree built from another lockfile and pass a stale install. A miss means a cold provision.
102: - **The provisioning walk runs on a hit.** The repository's own `provision_worktree` still runs after a restore and checks that each tree and each build output exists, so a hit shortens the install and is never a version check.
103: - **The cache is saved only on a miss**, and an input named `cache` set to `false` forces a cold provision so the install path stays exercised.
104: - **Bun comes from a SHA-pinned setup action**, never from an `npm install` of bun in the workflow.
105: - **The scan reads it.** `.github/scripts/check-gate-inputs.sh:499-503` (the `if [[ -d "$ROOT/.github/actions" ]]` block) scans `.github/actions/**` with the workflow parser, so a path in an action is held to the twin rule.
106: 
107: Today five jobs in three workflows call the action: `opencode-dual-version.yml` at `:113` and `:192`, `opencode-plugin-tests.yml` at `:92` and `routing-registry-drift.yml` at `:141` and `:248`. A new provisioning workflow calls the action and does not copy its steps.
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ## 6. THE SWITCH IF SHAPE
112: 
113: A job can be switched off from repository variables with one condition between `name:` and `runs-on:`. With no variable set, everything runs. A switch is any repository variable the condition compares against `off`, so `/doctor:ci report` reads any repository's names. The profile's `switch.master` and `switch.groups` name them, and the example below uses neutral names.
114: 
115: ```yaml
116: jobs:
117:   example:
118:     name: Example job
119:     if: vars.ACME_CI != 'off' && vars.ACME_CI_TESTS != 'off'
120:     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
121: ```
122: 
123: Skilled example: `if: vars.SKILLED_CI != 'off' && vars.SKILLED_CI_FRESHNESS != 'off'`.
124: 
125: - The condition is **job-level**, because `on:` filters see no contexts.
126: - Where a job already has a condition, the switch is ANDed onto it and never replaces it.
127: - `off` is the only disable token. `0`, `false` or a typo leaves the job on. That is fail-safe and must be documented wherever the variables are described.
128: - A job whose status context the branch ruleset requires is never switched off, and the other protected workflows follow `references/protected-set.md`.
129: - A workflow in the profile's `switch.exempt` gets no switch. When `switch.required` is true, every other job carries one.
130: - Skilled example: `SKILLED_CI` is the master switch. The five group switches are `SKILLED_CI_TESTS`, `SKILLED_CI_REPORTS`, `SKILLED_CI_REVIEW`, `SKILLED_CI_FRESHNESS` and `SKILLED_CI_MESSAGES`.
131: - Skilled example: `message-contract.yml` holds the required context, and `dependabot-auto-merge.yml` is the exempt workflow.
132: 
133: Skilled example: the shape is the rule. Today 42 of the 44 jobs carry it, and all 42 test `SKILLED_CI`. The group variables split as 24 on `SKILLED_CI_TESTS`, 11 on `SKILLED_CI_FRESHNESS`, 3 on `SKILLED_CI_REVIEW`, 3 on `SKILLED_CI_REPORTS` and 1 on `SKILLED_CI_MESSAGES`. Three jobs AND the switch onto an existing condition: `skill-doc-frontmatter.yml:67`, `trigger-index-rebuild.yml:33` and `trigger-index-rebuild.yml:189`. The two jobs without the switch are the `metadata` and `auto-merge` jobs of `dependabot-auto-merge.yml`, so a reader who finds no switch there is reading the current tree and not a gap in this file.
134:

65: Enforcement: honour-system.

69: ## 4. CONCURRENCY
70: 
71: A workflow that answers to pushes and pull requests carries one group, so a newer push does not leave an older run burning minutes.
72: 
73: ```yaml
74: concurrency:
75:   group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
76:   cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
77: ```

80:

49: 
50: The trigger-index rebuild workflow commits four generated files to the branch it ran on. No downstream workflow reads them as an input, so every other workflow that answers to a push would run for nothing.
51: 
52: **The rule.** A rebuild commit carries `[skip ci]` in its message body. 58: - `.github/workflows/trigger-index-rebuild.yml:33` guards the rebuild job itself with the `Trigger-Index-Rebuild: ci` trailer, so a run GitHub creates anyway does not rebuild a rebuild.
59:

70: A rule that ignores generated paths is push-only.

80: A trigger that departs from the norm for a reason is recorded here so a review or a report reads it as intentional and not as drift. 2: title: Repository CI Profile and Protected Workflows
3: description: The repository CI profile the /doctor:ci routes read, the workflows protected by function and the rules that follow, with this repository's Skilled profile as a labelled section.
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "protected workflow"
6:   - "protected workflow set"
7:   - "required status check"
8:   - "never switch off workflow"
9:   - "repository ci profile"
10: importance_tier: normal
11: contextType: general
12: version: 1.1.2.0
13: ---
14: 
15: # Repository CI Profile and Protected Workflows
16: 
17: Where a repository states its own CI conventions, and which workflows are never weakened, edited or switched off on a light confirmation.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Two guards sit behind every CI change: the profile that holds a repository's own values, and the workflow set that carries an invariant no other check backs up. This reference states where each lives, so a reviewer can name what a change would weaken before it lands.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Before editing, switching off or scaffolding a workflow
30: - When `/doctor:ci report`, `scaffold` or `toggle` returns something the packet default does not explain
31: - When a new workflow takes on a job that an existing protected workflow already guards
32: 
33: ### The Profile
34: 
35: Branch names, switch variables, path twins, README tables and the setup action differ from one repository to the next, so no rule in this packet hard-codes them. A repository states them in one file, `repository/ci.json` in its `sk-code-ci` packet, and `/doctor:ci report`, `scaffold` and `toggle` read it through `.skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/lib/ci-profile.cjs`.
36: 
37: The lookup order is `--profile <path>`, then the file-scoped git config value `skcode.ciProfile`, then `repository/ci.json` in this packet, then a generic default. A `repository` field limits the file to the repository it names, so a copy shipped with the skills into another repository is ignored, and a file left at the former root-level `.sk-code/` path is refused rather than read. A named path that does not exist is an error and never falls back, because a typo would otherwise drop every protection without a word. An unknown key is an error too.
38: 
39: The generic default forces nothing. It requires no switch, checks no README row, assumes no branch and protects no workflow. A repository without a profile gets the parser checks that hold everywhere and nothing that only this repository needs. To start one, copy `assets/ci-profile.template.json`, which reads as the default, and fill in the keys that differ.
40: 
41: ### Profile Keys
42: 
43: | Key | What reads it | Default |
44: |---|---|---|
45: | `schemaVersion` | Every reader. It must be `1` | required |
46: | `defaultBranch` | The report's run list and the toggle's ruleset read. Without it the report asks GitHub, then falls back to `main` | `null` |
47: | `integrationBranches` | The scaffold's push `branches:` filter | `[]`, no filter |
48: | `workflowsReadme` | `{ path, rowTables }`. The report reads purposes from the README's `Workflow` and `Responsibility` table and flags a missing row. The scaffold prints one row per table. The toggle reads a `<NAME> must stay unset` sentence | `null`, no README check |
49: | `switch.master`, `switch.groups` | The switch variables, in the order the report lists them and the toggle accepts them. Without them the toggle accepts the names the workflows compare against `off` | `null`, `[]` |
50: | `switch.required` | Whether every job must carry a switch. Only then does the report flag `switch-missing` | `false` |
51: | `switch.exempt` | Workflow files that need no switch even when one is required | `[]` |
52: | `neverOff` | Variables the toggle never sets to `off`, whether or not the ruleset can be read | `[]` |
53: | `protected` | `{ file, role }` entries. The scaffold refuses the name and the toggle asks a second named confirmation before it switches one off | `[]` |
54: | `pathTwins` | `[root, twin]` pairs a path filter must name together | `[]`, no twin rule |
55: | `rebuildTrailer` | The commit trailer that marks a rebuild commit the report skips | `null`, nothing skipped |
56: | `setupAction` | `{ uses, with, note }` for the composite setup step the job template adds | `null`, no setup step |
57: | `timeoutFloorMinutes` | The timeout floor the templates start from | `10` |
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 2. PROTECTED BY FUNCTION
62: 
63: A workflow is protected because of what it does, so a new workflow that does the same job joins the set. Three classes qualify.
64: 
65: | Class | Test |
66: |---|---|
67: | (a) Sole enforcer | It is the only thing that enforces an invariant, and no local gate backs it up |
68: | (b) Token-eligibility split | It splits the work that runs repository code from the work that holds a write token |
69: | (c) Input guard | Its failure invalidates the inputs other workflows trust |
70: 
71: A workflow that holds a status context the branch ruleset requires is protected as well, because switching it off removes the requirement. The profile's `protected` list names the protected workflows with the role of each, and the toggle reads the required contexts from the live ruleset.
72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 3. THE RULES
76: 
77: 1. **Never switch off a job whose status context the branch ruleset requires.** A switched-off job is skipped, and a skipped job reports Success, so the required context stops blocking merges. A workflow-level path filter is the opposite case and leaves the context Pending (`references/trigger-and-filter-rules.md`). `/doctor:ci toggle` refuses such a variable from the live ruleset, from the profile's `neverOff` list and from a `must stay unset` sentence in the workflows README.
78: 2. **A protected workflow is never edited or switched off without a second named confirmation that restates its role.** The first confirmation approves the change. The second names the workflow, says in one sentence what it protects and approves again. `/doctor:ci toggle` asks it whenever a variable would switch off a workflow in the profile's `protected` list, and only the variable name counts as the answer. A scaffold or a review that would weaken a protected workflow stops and asks.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 4. HOW TO USE THE SET
83: 
84: - Before editing a workflow, search the profile's `protected` list for its file name and apply the class tests above.
85: - When a request reads "switch off", "skip" or "disable" a workflow, check rule 1 first.
86: - When two protected classes both fit, apply the stricter rule.
87: - When the list looks wrong for a workflow that was added or renamed, correct the profile and this file's Skilled section, and do not rely on memory.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ## 5. SKILLED PROFILE
92: 
93: This repository commits its profile as `repository/ci.json`. Everything in this section is the Skilled example, and none of it applies to another repository.
94: 
95: | Class | Workflows |
96: |---|---|
97: | (a) Sole enforcer | `gate-inputs.yml` |
98: | (b) Token-eligibility split | `trigger-index-rebuild.yml` |
99: | (c) Input guard | `dispatch-enforcement-guard.yml`, `naming-standard-guard.yml` |
100: | Required check | `message-contract.yml` |
101:

15: # Repository CI Profile and Protected Workflows
16: 
17: Where a repository states its own CI conventions, and which workflows are never weakened, edited or switched off on a light confirmation.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Two guards sit behind every CI change: the profile that holds a repository's own values, and the workflow set that carries an invariant no other check backs up. This reference states where each lives, so a reviewer can name what a change would weaken before it lands.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Before editing, switching off or scaffolding a workflow
30: - When `/doctor:ci report`, `scaffold` or `toggle` returns something the packet default does not explain
31: - When a new workflow takes on a job that an existing protected workflow already guards
32: 
33: ### The Profile
34: 
35: Branch names, switch variables, path twins, README tables and the setup action differ from one repository to the next, so no rule in this packet hard-codes them. A repository states them in one file, `repository/ci.json` in its `sk-code-ci` packet, and `/doctor:ci report`, `scaffold` and `toggle` read it through `.skilled/commands/doctor/scripts/lib/ci-profile.cjs`.
36: 
37: The lookup order is `--profile <path>`, then the file-scoped git config value `skcode.ciProfile`, then `repository/ci.json` in this packet, then a generic default. A `repository` field limits the file to the repository it names, so a copy shipped with the skills into another repository is ignored, and a file left at the former root-level `.sk-code/` path is refused rather than read. A named path that does not exist is an error and never falls back, because a typo would otherwise drop every protection without a word. An unknown key is an error too.
38: 
39: The generic default forces nothing. It requires no switch, checks no README row, assumes no branch and protects no workflow. A repository without a profile gets the parser checks that hold everywhere and nothing that only this repository needs. To start one, copy `assets/ci-profile.template.json`, which reads as the default, and fill in the keys that differ.
40: 
41: ### Profile Keys
42: 
43: | Key | What reads it | Default |
44: |---|---|---|
45: | `schemaVersion` | Every reader. It must be `1` | required |
46: | `defaultBranch` | The report's run list and the toggle's ruleset read. Without it the report asks GitHub, then falls back to `main` | `null` |
47: | `integrationBranches` | The scaffold's push `branches:` filter | `[]`, no filter |
48: | `workflowsReadme` | `{ path, rowTables }`. The report reads purposes from the README's `Workflow` and `Responsibility` table and flags a missing row. The scaffold prints one row per table. The toggle reads a `<NAME> must stay unset` sentence | `null`, no README check |
49: | `switch.master`, `switch.groups` | The switch variables, in the order the report lists them and the toggle accepts them. Without them the toggle accepts the names the workflows compare against `off` | `null`, `[]` |
50: | `switch.required` | Whether every job must carry a switch. Only then does the report flag `switch-missing` | `false` |
51: | `switch.exempt` | Workflow files that need no switch even when one is required | `[]` |
52: | `neverOff` | Variables the toggle never sets to `off`, whether or not the ruleset can be read | `[]` |
53: | `protected` | `{ file, role }` entries. The scaffold refuses the name and the toggle asks a second named confirmation before it switches one off | `[]` |
54: | `pathTwins` | `[root, twin]` pairs a path filter must name together | `[]`, no twin rule |
55: | `rebuildTrailer` | The commit trailer that marks a rebuild commit the report skips | `null`, nothing skipped |
56: | `setupAction` | `{ uses, with, note }` for the composite setup step the job template adds | `null`, no setup step |
57: | `timeoutFloorMinutes` | The timeout floor the templates start from | `10` |
58: 
59: ---
60: 
61: ## 2. PROTECTED BY FUNCTION
62: 
63: A workflow is protected because of what it does, so a new workflow that does the same job joins the set. Three classes qualify.
64: 
65: | Class | Test |
66: |---|---|
67: | (a) Sole enforcer | It is the only thing that enforces an invariant, and no local gate backs it up |
68: | (b) Token-eligibility split | It splits the work that runs repository code from the work that holds a write token |
69: | (c) Input guard | Its failure invalidates the inputs other workflows trust |
70:

72: 
73: ---
74: 
75: ## 3. THE RULES
76: 
77: 1. **Never switch off a job whose status context the branch ruleset requires.** A switched-off job is skipped, and a skipped job reports Success, so the required context stops blocking merges. 78: 2. **A protected workflow is never edited or switched off without a second named confirmation that restates its role.** The first confirmation approves the change. The second names the workflow, says in one sentence what it protects and approves again. `/doctor:ci toggle` asks it whenever a variable would switch off a workflow in the profile's `protected` list, and only the variable name counts as the answer. A scaffold or a review that would weaken a protected workflow stops and asks.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 4. HOW TO USE THE SET
83: 
84: - Before editing a workflow, search the profile's `protected` list for its file name and apply the class tests above.
85: - When a request reads "switch off", "skip" or "disable" a workflow, check rule 1 first.
86: - When two protected classes both fit, apply the stricter rule.

88: 
89: ---
90:

98: | (b) Token-eligibility split | `trigger-index-rebuild.yml` |
99: | (c) Input guard | `dispatch-enforcement-guard.yml`, `naming-standard-guard.yml` |
100: | Required check | `message-contract.yml` |

23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: The smart router maps a detected surface (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) plus a classified intent (IMPLEMENTATION / DEBUGGING / VERIFICATION / etc.) to the exact references, assets, and verification commands needed for the active task. 32: - When mapping intent to concrete reference paths
33: - When picking verification commands for the surface
34: 
35: ### Core Principle
36: 
37: Routing is a two-stage decision: **surface-first, intent-second**. Surface narrows the resource family: a declared specific surface first, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN. Intent narrows the specific files within that family. The detected surface also goes to the compiled front door as `--surface-hint`. When a prompt ties between surfaces, a hinted specific surface leads the bundle. SKILLED already ranks last, so a SKILLED hint changes nothing (`SKILL.md` §3).

48:

# sk-code Surface Router — routing logic and resource maps

Leaf-set authority for sk-code. The routing authority is named once in `SKILL.md` §2 SMART ROUTING: `hub-router.json` is the mode vocabulary, and this document is the leaf-set router. Consolidates intent classification + resource loading into the single Barter-style smart-routing entry point. Detection logic lives in [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md); phase lifecycle lives in [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md).

---

## 1. OVERVIEW

### Purpose

The smart router maps a detected surface (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) plus a classified intent (IMPLEMENTATION / DEBUGGING / VERIFICATION / etc.) to the exact references, assets, and verification commands needed for the active task. Loads only the smallest relevant set so the active context window stays focused.

### When to Use

- After surface detection (see [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md)) determines the surface: a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN
- When classifying task wording into the dominant work intent
- When mapping intent to concrete reference paths
- When picking verification commands for the surface

### Core Principle

Routing is a two-stage decision: **surface-first, intent-second**. Surface narrows the resource family: a declared specific surface first, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN. Intent narrows the specific files within that family. The detected surface also goes to the compiled front door as `--surface-hint`. When a prompt ties between surfaces, a hinted specific surface leads the bundle. SKILLED already ranks last, so a SKILLED hint changes nothing (`SKILL.md` §3).

### Key Sources

- [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md): surface detection (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) and SKILLED language sub-detection
- [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md) — Phase 1/2/3 lifecycle and phase-specific resource expectations
- `SKILL.md` §2 SMART ROUTING — names the routing authority split and the compiled front door

---

## 2. INTENT MODEL

Intent classification scores task text against weighted keyword signals to pick the dominant work type after surface detection. The vocabulary and weights are authored once, in the `INTENT_SIGNALS` block of §8 MACHINE-READABLE ROUTER; read them there. This section is the human-facing summary of how that block is scored, never a second copy of its keywords.


## 10. RELATED RESOURCES

- [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md): surface detection (a declared specific surface, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN) + SKILLED language sub-detection
- [`phase-detection.md`](shared/references/phase-detection.md) — Phase 1/2/3 lifecycle and per-phase resource loading
- `SKILL.md` §2 SMART ROUTING — names the routing authority split and the compiled front door
- Barter equivalent: `barter/.skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/references/smart-routing.md` (different routing key — git-remote project — but same structural pattern)

---

## 11. MACHINE ROUTER

The hub's detailed routing prose, moved here from `SKILL.md` so the skill body keeps only a short routing summary and a pointer to this file. It sits last, after the stage-two map above, and it declares no map of its own: the `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` block in section 8 stays the only replay source.

> **Compiled routing (default-on, flag-gated, additive).** Resolve the mode via the compiled router contract first:
> ```bash
> node .skilled/bin/compiled-route.cjs --hub sk-code --prompt "<task>"
> ```
> Follow the returned decision: `route` (use its `targets`), `clarify`/`defer` (disambiguate) or `reject` (refuse). On a `{"servingAuthority":"legacy"}` sentinel or any error, use the routing below. The front door self-gates on serving-authority. Compiled routing is now the default for `sk-code`. Set `SPECKIT_COMPILED_ROUTING=0`, the explicit kill-switch, to force legacy routing fleet-wide.

**Session surface hint.** Before you call the front door, run the surface detection in [`stack-detection.md`](shared/references/stack-detection.md) on the session's working directory and the files it is editing.
Then add its result as `--surface-hint <SURFACE>`, for example `--surface-hint SKILLED`.
When the prompt's keywords tie between surfaces, a hinted specific surface leads them.
Workflow modes keep first place, and the targets and the bundle kind stay the same.
`SKILLED` is the fallback surface and always ranks last, so a `SKILLED` hint changes nothing.
With `UNKNOWN`, no hint or a surface the prompt did not match, the `routerPolicy.tieBreak` order applies.

### Surface Router: per-intent leaf sets

Root `ROUTER.md` owns the second-stage `INTENT_SIGNALS` / `RESOURCE_MAP`, while packet-owned resources stay typed through `leaf-manifest.json`.
The hub-level shared controls are declared once, in `ROUTER.md` §8: the `SHARED_CONTROL_RESOURCES` list plus the always-loaded `DEFAULT_RESOURCE` preamble. They resolve on disk but never project as leaves.
The hub router keeps stage-one mode selection and its `shared/README.md` fallback.

### The discriminator
- **`workflowMode`** - the public mode/packet key: `sk-code-quality`, `sk-code-review` (workflow) or `sk-code-ci`, `sk-code-frontend`, `sk-code-skilled` (surface).
- **`packetKind`** - the axis: `workflow` (a mode that acts) or `surface` (read-only evidence bundled alongside a mode).

# sk-code-frontend

> Frontend guidance for web work, with a five-pass check for comparing a built screen with its Figma frame.

---

## 1. AT A GLANCE

| Aspect | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Packet kind** | `surface`, backend `evidence-base`, read-only |
| **Tools** | `Read, Bash, Grep, Glob` |
| **Use it for** | Web markup and CSS, web accessibility, and Figma-to-code checks |
| **Invoke with** | No direct invocation. The sk-code hub bundles it beside a workflow mode when frontend evidence applies, or routes it alone when no workflow mode scores |
| **Advisor** | Invisible (`routingClass: metadata`) |
| **Bundled with** | `sk-code-quality` for authoring and `sk-code-review` for review, or routed alone |
| **Produces** | Shared principles, web guidance, topic references, and the five-pass Figma check; the packet edits nothing |

---

## 2. OVERVIEW

### Why This Surface Exists

Frontend work needs shared rules that hold across frameworks, with a web layer for the mechanics the web platform uses. A design frame also needs a consistent check against the built screen without copying its layer tree into code.

### What It Holds

[`references/frontend-practice.md`](references/frontend-practice.md) is the core page for shared principles, token guidance, Figma as reference, and overrides. The web layer is [`references/web-markup-and-css.md`](references/web-markup-and-css.md). Six web topic files provide focused guidance, and [`references/figma-to-code.md`](references/figma-to-code.md) defines the five-pass check and its verdicts.

The packet is read-only. The paired workflow mode applies its evidence to the requested work.

---

## 3. REFERENCE MAP

| File | Carries |
|---|---|
| `references/frontend-practice.md` | Shared principles, token precedence, the Figma boundary, and the Frontend overrides contract |
| `references/web-markup-and-css.md` | Semantic web markup, forms, layout, responsive behavior, media, CSS architecture, and framework examples |
| Six web topic files | Elements and attributes, cascade and selectors, layout and sizing, accessibility patterns, performance and loading, and internationalization |
| `references/figma-to-code.md` | Read-only inputs, five passes, the verdict and report, and the Figma-side tool ladder |
| `manual-testing-playbook/` | The routing scenarios the hub's router-sync guard replays: one web and one Figma check |
| `references/workflow-*.md` | Shared implement, debug, and verify workflow doctrine |

The packet router lists each topic file and the condition that calls for it.

---

## 4. VERIFICATION

| Check | How to run it |
|---|---|
| Packet contents | `ls -la .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/references` |
| Router declarations | `rg -n "## 3\. MACHINE ROUTER|^INTENT_SIGNALS|^RESOURCE_MAP|^DEFAULT_RESOURCE" .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/ROUTER.md` |
| Playbook package | `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-manual-testing-playbook/scripts/validate-playbook-package.cjs --package .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/manual-testing-playbook` |

The listing shows the web and topic references plus the three shared workflow links. The router check prints the machine-router heading and its resource declarations. The playbook check reports the two scenarios and exits 0.

---

## 5. RELATED DOCUMENTS

| Document | Why to read it |
|---|---|
| [SKILL.md](SKILL.md) | Surface identity, bundling conditions, and the overrides contract |
| [ROUTER.md](ROUTER.md) | Intent map, topic-file conditions, and machine router |
| [../SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) | The sk-code hub that bundles this surface beside a workflow mode |
| [references/frontend-practice.md](references/frontend-practice.md) | Shared principles and the Frontend overrides contract |
| [references/figma-to-code.md](references/figma-to-code.md) | The five-pass check for a built screen and its Figma frame |
| [manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md](manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md) | Manual scenarios that validate the web and Figma-check routing |

12: 
13: # Frontend Surface: Stack-Agnostic Web Practice
14: 
15: Read-only frontend evidence for web work across project stacks.
16: 
17: ## 1. WHEN THE HUB BUNDLES THIS
18: 
19: The sk-code hub bundles this surface beside `sk-code-quality` for authoring or `sk-code-review` for review when a request needs shared web frontend practice, or a Figma-to-code check, and it routes this surface alone when no workflow mode scores.
20: 
21: This packet writes nothing. When the hub bundles it beside a workflow mode, that mode applies the guidance it loads. When no workflow mode scores, the hub routes this packet alone, and the acting agent applies the guidance and hands the author gates to `sk-code-quality` before it claims completion.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 2. REFERENCE MAP
26: 
27: - [`references/frontend-practice.md`](references/frontend-practice.md) holds the shared principles and the Frontend overrides contract.
28: - [`references/web-markup-and-css.md`](references/web-markup-and-css.md) is the web layer.
29: - The six web topic files cover focused implementation details for web work.
30: - [`references/figma-to-code.md`](references/figma-to-code.md) holds the five-pass check for comparing a built screen with its Figma frame.
31: - [`references/workflow-implement.md`](references/workflow-implement.md), [`references/workflow-debug.md`](references/workflow-debug.md), and [`references/workflow-verify.md`](references/workflow-verify.md) provide the shared workflow doctrine.
32: 
33: ### Manual Testing Playbook
34: 
35: Manual testing scenarios for this surface live in [`manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md`](manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md), the root index, plus one file per intent family under `manual-testing-playbook/frontend-surface/<scenario>.md`. The category folder and each scenario file use bare descriptive slugs, with no numeric prefix.
36: Each scenario declares the `expected_intent` and `expected_resources` the packet router emits for its exact prompt, so the hub's router-sync guard replays both.
37: 
38: Validate the package with the operator-scenario contract:
39: `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-manual-testing-playbook/scripts/validate-playbook-package.cjs --package .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/manual-testing-playbook`
40: 
41: ---
42: 
43: ## 3. SMART ROUTING
44: 
45: Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) for the intent map, topic-file loading conditions, and machine router. The core loads by default, followed by the matching web or Figma-to-code reference.
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 4. SURFACE STANDARDS
50: 
51: ### ✅ ALWAYS
52: 
53: - Read the shared principles and the web layer before applying a topic reference.
54: - Load a topic file when its condition in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) applies.
55: - Use installed design tokens and report a missing token instead of inventing a value.
56: - Mark a Figma pass `NOT RUN` with its reason; the overall verdict is `INCOMPLETE` when any pass cannot run.
57: 
58: ### ⛔ NEVER
59: 
60: - Write, edit, or scaffold through this packet. The acting workflow mode applies any change.
61: - Treat a Figma layer tree as the code structure.
62: 
63: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
64: 
65: - Project conventions conflict with a core or web-layer statement; record the decision under the mode's Frontend overrides heading.
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 5. FRONTEND OVERRIDES
70: 
71: A project mode records each change to a core or web-layer statement under a `Frontend overrides` heading in its own `SKILL.md`, naming the section, whether it replaces, extends, or disables the statement, and the reason; when nothing differs, it says that it follows the core and web layer unchanged. Its completion report names the overrides it applied. See [Frontend practice, Section 5](references/frontend-practice.md#5-overrides).
